claims.text: Conventional powder metallurgy can leave noble-metal HEA nanomaterials with local elemental segregation.
Controlled deposition produces more uniform nanoscale elemental mixing than powder metallurgy.
Controlled deposition suppresses phase segregation relative to powder metallurgy.
Greater elemental homogeneity and reduced phase segregation enhance catalytic performance by producing a consistent distribution of active sites.
Deposition rapidly quenches diffusion and phase separation during synthesis.
Rapid quenching during deposition enforces kinetically controlled mixing of multiple noble metals.
Homogeneous noble-metal mixing maintains a high density and consistent distribution of catalytically active sites.
A high density and consistent distribution of active sites are important for reactions such as the oxygen reduction reaction.
Under identical testing conditions, deposition-synthesized HEA nanomaterials will have a statistically significant catalytic-performance advantage over powder-metallurgy samples.
Deposition-synthesized HEA nanomaterials will exhibit higher turnover frequency than powder-metallurgy samples.
Deposition-synthesized HEA nanomaterials will exhibit lower onset potential than powder-metallurgy samples.
The proposed mechanism should apply to noble-metal HEA nanomaterials made under controlled temperature and quenching conditions typical of deposition.
The proposed performance relationship should apply to reactions in which active-site uniformity critically influences performance.
Poorly maintained deposition conditions or alloy systems with extremely rapid phase-separation kinetics may fall outside the hypothesis.
The magnitude of catalytic improvement may vary with the noble-metal combination and deposition parameters.
